content: International Nurses Day (IND) is observed globally on May 12 each year to honor the significant contributions that nurses make to society. The International Council of Nurses (ICN) has been commemorating this day since 1965. In 1953, Dorothy Sutherland, an official from the U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, proposed to President Eisenhower that a Nurses Day be proclaimed, but the proposal was not approved. In January 1974, it was decided to celebrate International Nurses Day on May 12, marking the birth anniversary of Florence Nightingale, who is widely regarded as the founder of modern nursing. Each year, the ICN develops and distributes an International Nurses' Day Kit, which includes educational and public information materials for nurses worldwide. However, Florence Nightingale is no longer universally regarded as a role model in some regions. For instance, the British public sector union UNISON has advocated for changing the date of the celebration. One alternative proposed is May 21, the birthday of Elizabeth Fry (1780–1845), who founded the Institution of Nursing Sisters and is also recognized for her work with prisoners. In addition to International Nurses Day, May 8 has been designated as National Student Nurses Day in the United States since 1998, and it is celebrated annually. Furthermore, since 2003, National School Nurse Day has been observed on the Wednesday within National Nurses Week, which runs from May 6 to May 12 each year. In the United Kingdom, a service is held annually on May 12 at Westminster Abbey in London. During this service, a symbolic lamp is taken from the Nurses' Chapel in the Abbey and passed from one nurse to another before being handed to the Dean, who places it on the High Altar. This act symbolizes the transfer of knowledge from one nurse to another. Additionally, a service is held at St. Margaret's Church in East Wellow, Hampshire, where Florence Nightingale is buried, on the Sunday following her birthday. The ICN has introduced specific themes for International Nurses Day over the years, focusing on various aspects of health and nursing. Examples include Safe Motherhood in 1988, Mental Health Nurses in Action in 1991, Healthy Ageing in 1992, and Nurses: Fighting AIDS stigma, working for all in 2003. Other themes have addressed issues such as women's health, patient safety, and the importance of positive practice environments. In the United States and Canada, National Nursing Week is celebrated annually from May 9 to May 15. This observance was established in the United States by President Richard Nixon in 1974.
